<<7:172 update 1, part 0 of 0..4>>
## THE CURRENT MAP
7:172/q01 What does 'when' ask the audience to recall? [وَإِذْ · grammar]
  7:172/q01/p1 It is the object of an omitted command to remember the covenant. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj makes idh accusative; Ibn Ashur calls it past time, not an adverb. Islahi treats it as recalling a definite, though forgotten, event.
7:172/q02 What does God's taking mean here? [أَخَذَ · meaning] (turns on: Whether taking denotes extraction, God's encompassing possession, or the binding covenant; the surrounding wording and reported scene guide the reading.)
  7:172/q02/p1 God extracted or brought offspring into being from their forebears. — reasons: Ibn Ashur compares 6:46. Tabatabai says taking separates offspring without diminishing the source, yielding distinct accountable persons.
  7:172/q02/p2 Taking is encompassing and ownership. — reasons: Tabatabai connects it with God's proof over all creatures.
  7:172/q02/p3 It is the binding imposition of a covenant, figured as a weight on the back. — reasons: Abu Hayyan cites covenant formulas at 4:154 and 2:83 and specifies monotheism and exclusive worship.
  7:172/q02/p4 Divine taking brings the nonexistent into existence by God's power. — reasons: The Najmiyya distinguishes God's creation from a creature's taking an existing thing; it cites 19:9.
7:172/q03 Who are the children of Adam addressed in the covenant? [بَنِىٓ ءَادَمَ · referent] (turns on: The plural backs and the following excuse about polytheist ancestors are read either as specifying a subgroup or as part of an account embracing every human.)
  7:172/q03/p1 All humanity through the final generation is included. — reasons: Ubayy's report includes everyone born before the Hour; Alusi rejects a restriction to Jewish ancestors. Tabatabai argues otherwise untaken persons could plead ignorance.
  7:172/q03/p2 Only certain descendants, particularly those with idolatrous ancestors or reached by prophets, are meant. — reasons: The plural backs excludes Adam's immediate children, and the next verse's ancestral-shirk excuse narrows the group; Bursevi excludes people who had no offspring.
  7:172/q03/p3 The messengers were specifically addressed. — reasons: Abd al-Malik ibn Abi Yazid and Wahb ibn Munabbih are named for this view.
7:172/q04 How is 'from their backs' related to 'children of Adam'? [مِنۢ بَنِىٓ ءَادَمَ مِن ظُهُورِهِمْ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the plural backs is simply an appositive account of generational origin or excludes the Adam-back account.)
  7:172/q04/p1 The latter is a partitive apposition specifying the former: descendants are drawn from human fathers' backs. — reasons: The repeated min reinforces apposition; Samīn cites analogous part-whole idiom, while Ibn Ashur cites 6:99. Alusi prefers the partitive parsing.
  7:172/q04/p2 The apposition is of inclusion, relating bodies or members to the people. — reasons: Abu al-Baqa gives this parsing; Alusi questions its rationale.
  7:172/q04/p3 The wording describes successive generations, so Adam's own back need not be repeated. — reasons: Al-Kinani and others say all are Adam's offspring and descend through one another; Ibn Ashur argues Adam's immediate children are included a fortiori.
  7:172/q04/p4 The plural backs specifically excludes a direct taking from Adam's single back as the verse's meaning. — reasons: The Mu'tazilites and Tabarsi stress the plural nouns; Ibn Atiyya considers a root-and-branch reconciliation weak.
7:172/q05 What happened when the descendants were taken and addressed? [أَخَذَ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ وَأَشْهَدَهُمْ · interpretation] (turns on: The grammatical contrast between Adam's back and descendants' backs, the status of extraction reports, whether pre-birth testimony could be remembered and serve as proof, and whether speech can be real outside ordinary bodily life.)
  7:172/q05/p1 God actually extracted Adam's progeny before earthly life and elicited a spoken covenant. — reasons: Reports describe a touch, stroke, shoulder strike, combing or scattering; particles or formed spirits were given understanding. Al-Zajjaj invokes the speaking ant and praising mountains; Tabatabai argues speech can be real beyond ordinary organs. Razi and Ibn Atiyya defend combining the verse with the reports.
  7:172/q05/p2 The dialogue represents natural generation and the rational recognition of God's oneness from signs. — reasons: Zamakhshari compares 41:11 and 16:40; poems personify limbs and the wind. Tabarsi also cites 9:17. Ibn Kathir cites circumstantial testimony at 6:130 and 9:17 and stresses the plural backs. Abu Hayyan finds the hadith reconcilations strained. Bursevi treats the exchange as signs in souls and horizons.
  7:172/q05/p3 Humanity truly witnessed in a prior divine realm whose precedence is not ordinary chronological pre-birth life. — reasons: Tabatabai distinguishes measured worldly unfolding from the complete existence with God in 15:21, 36:82–83 and 54:50; the same humanity witnesses directly in malakut. He rejects identifying later persons with tiny bodily particles.
  7:172/q05/p4 The covenant was taken from souls before their bodies were created. — reasons: Muhammad ibn Ka'b and others report pre-body acknowledgment; one view locates it in Paradise and another after descent. The Study Quran identifies this as a pretemporal pact.
  7:172/q05/p5 Affirm the covenant without fixing its unseen mechanism. — reasons: Kuranyolu says the duty is to accept that humans can know God's lordship and keep the pledge, since precise unseen details exceed human knowledge.
7:172/q06 Where was the primordial extraction said to occur? [أَخَذَ رَبُّكَ · reports] (turns on: The geographical and descent-stage variants in transmitted reports; Alusi questions the basis of India and Kaaba locations.)
  7:172/q06/p1 At Nu'man near Arafah. — reasons: Prophetic and Ibn Abbas reports identify the valley; variants call it Batn or Wadi Nu'man and connect it with the Day of Arafah.
  7:172/q06/p2 In India, where Adam descended. — reasons: Reports vary among Dajni, Dahna, Barhaba and Rahba; Ibn Atiyya also mentions Sind.
  7:172/q06/p3 Between Mecca and Taif. — reasons: Al-Kalbi and Muqatil are named for this site.
  7:172/q06/p4 In heaven or Paradise before descent. — reasons: Some reports specify the lowest heaven; others Paradise or heaven generally.
  7:172/q06/p5 At the Kaaba, with particle-like descendants surrounding Adam. — reasons: Alusi reports this location but says it and India lack a dependable basis.
7:172/q07 When did the covenant occur relative to Adam's descent and human births? [وَإِذْ أَخَذَ · reports] (turns on: Reports place Adam before or after descent, while interpretive readings locate the covenant in birth, prior non-temporal existence, or more than one event.)
  7:172/q07/p1 Before Adam's descent from Paradise. — reasons: Al-Suddi places it in the lowest heaven; some place it in Paradise. Reports also give a time when the Throne was over water.
  7:172/q07/p2 After Adam's descent to earth. — reasons: Reports locate the event at Arafah or in India after descent; some say Adam was in water when descendants emerged.
  7:172/q07/p3 As each person develops in the father's loins or mother's womb, and later reaches understanding. — reasons: This is the worldly, generational reading; Kuranyolu distinguishes possible stages of the innate endowment.
  7:172/q07/p4 Before spirits were breathed into the descendants' bodies. — reasons: Islahi calls it an actual event, with innate cognizance lasting after the occasion is forgotten.
  7:172/q07/p5 There were multiple covenant-taking events or kinds of covenant. — reasons: Sufi masters propose this to reconcile reports, while Alusi says their language suggests different kinds; Al-Shirazi distinguishes present rational from primordial verbal covenant.
7:172/q08 What became of the extracted descendants before their earthly births? [ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ · reports]
  7:172/q08/p1 God returned them to Adam's or their fathers' loins, and each decreed person would be born. — reasons: Ibn Abbas says their number neither increases nor decreases and the Hour waits for all who testified. Reports differ on whether the return is to Adam alone or successive fathers.
7:172/q09 What does the word 'offspring' mean and how is it derived? [ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ · meaning] (turns on: Proposed roots connect the word either to small scattered particles or to God's act of creating.)
  7:172/q09/p1 It means progeny and can denote one person, a group, or a collective. — reasons: Abu Ali compares the individual in Zechariah's prayer (3:38–39; 19:5–7) and collective bashar (12:31; 64:6; 14:10).
  7:172/q09/p2 It derives from dharr, tiny scattered particles or ants. — reasons: Proposals include faʿūlūla with rāʾ changed to yāʾ, faʿīla resolving doubling, and a nisba with fatḥa changed to ḍamma; the narrative pictures particles or seeds.
  7:172/q09/p3 It derives from dhara'a, to bring creatures into being and make them manifest. — reasons: Abu Ali compares the contracted form al-bariyya; one further proposal invokes the scattering winds of 18:45.
7:172/q10 How is 'their offspring' read? [ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ · readings] (turns on: Whether the collective singular sufficiently conveys all offspring or a plural better marks the many generations.)
  7:172/q10/p1 It is read as singular dhurriyyatahum, collective in sense. — reasons: Ibn Kathir, Asim, Hamza and Kisai, or Mecca and Kufa, use it; its collective force is compared with bashar and 24:31. Nashr notes the pattern across Yasin and al-Tur.
  7:172/q10/p2 It is read as plural dhurriyyatihim, explicitly covering multiple generations. — reasons: Nafi, Abu Amr, Ibn Amir and in some enumerations Abu Jafar or Yaqub use it. Broken plurals can be pluralized; the plural fits zuhurihim.
  7:172/q10/p3 A reported reading has singular dhurriyyatahu, referring to Adam. — reasons: Al-Kashshaf records it without a named reader.
7:172/q11 What is the grammatical object of 'took'? [أَخَذَ ذُرِّيَّتَه
<<part 0 ends; continues in part 1>>

<<7:172 update 1, part 1 of 0..4>>
ُمْ · grammar] (turns on: Whether the verb directly takes the descendants or has an unspoken covenant as its object; the singular and plural readings affect case marking.)
  7:172/q11/p1 Their offspring is the direct object. — reasons: Al-Hawfi and Samīn use this straightforward parsing; Jishumi notes a form-dependent case analysis.
  7:172/q11/p2 An omitted 'covenant' is the object, with offspring appositional or an omitted genitive. — reasons: Ibn Atiyya and Abu Hayyan supply the covenant; Samīn says the singular needs an omitted annexed noun, while the feminine plural permits genitive apposition.
7:172/q12 Why use these words and this order for the taking? [أَخَذَ مِن ظُهُورِهِمْ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ · rhetoric]
  7:172/q12/p1 The wording dignifies and strengthens the covenant and gives prominence to the descendants. — reasons: Alusi says 'took' signals selection and covenantal gravity; Biqai sees fathers' strong backs and human capacity; Alusi says delaying the object creates anticipation and keeps its pronoun after its antecedent.
7:172/q13 How did God make people witness against themselves? [وَأَشْهَدَهُمْ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether witnessing is personal verbal confession, reciprocal testimony, innate rational evidence, or immediate experience in a prior realm.)
  7:172/q13/p1 He made each confess personally that He alone is Lord. — reasons: Muqatil, Ibn Bahr and Bursevi stress self-testimony; Tabatabai says God showed people the reality of their dependent selves. The preposition can mean witness against oneself.
  7:172/q13/p2 Some descendants testified to the acknowledgment of others. — reasons: Tabari prefers this apparent meaning if the disputed Prophetic wording is unsound; Ibn Abbas and Ubayy are also cited. A pause at bala is then generally unsuitable.
  7:172/q13/p3 God established innate knowledge and rational signs, so their selves testify by their condition. — reasons: Zamakhshari, Nasafi and others treat the encounter as representation; Ibn Kathir compares circumstantial witness in 6:130, 9:17, 100:7 and 14:34. Biqai includes miracles and messengers among the proofs.
  7:172/q13/p4 God made direct witnessing of His lordship possible in a prior realm. — reasons: Tabatabai reads the knowledge as immediate experience, with the self, tongue and heart aligned; some Imami reports say knowledge was fixed even when the scene was forgotten.
7:172/q14 What does 'Am I not your Lord?' assert? [أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ · rhetoric] (turns on: Whether the confirmation is a figurative depiction of evidence or an actual communication in an unseen mode.)
  7:172/q14/p1 It is a confirmatory question demanding acknowledgment of God's exclusive lordship. — reasons: Al-Zajjaj and Thalabi call it confirmation; Bursevi and Alusi explain Lord as unrestricted master and nurturer. Ibn Ashur compares 46:34; Bint al-Shati notes interrogative laysa with prefixed bā emphatically affirms.
  7:172/q14/p2 The question is genuine creative communication, even if no ordinary voice or bodily organ was involved. — reasons: Tabatabai defines speech as conveying an intended meaning; God created a form able to answer.
7:172/q15 What did the descendants' answer affirm, and how was it given? [قَالُوا۟ بَلَىٰ · interpretation] (turns on: Whether the primordial response was equally sincere in all or already differentiated the blessed and the wretched.)
  7:172/q15/p1 They acknowledged God alone as Lord and their own servanthood, worship and obedience. — reasons: Some reports include the prohibition of shirk, a pledge to obey, and God's provision; Islahi stresses lordship and providence rather than bare deity.
  7:172/q15/p2 The blessed answered freely and sincerely, while the wretched answered reluctantly or deceptively. — reasons: Al-Suddi and others connect this with willing and unwilling submission in 3:83; Bursevi's Najmiyya places the forerunners, right and left in different spiritual modes.
  7:172/q15/p3 All answered truly or had a universal capacity to acknowledge God. — reasons: Study Quran reports rejection of reluctant testimony and prefers the verse's shared possibility of recognition; Tabatabai says heart and tongue were one in the prior realm.
7:172/q16 Why did they answer with 'balā', and what would 'naʿam' mean? [بَلَىٰ · grammar] (turns on: Whether response follows the question's negative form, its affirmative intent, or ordinary usage allowing an ambiguous naʿam.)
  7:172/q16/p1 Balā cancels the negative wording and unambiguously affirms God is Lord; naʿam would confirm the negation and mean disbelief. — reasons: Al-Farra and reports from Ibn Abbas stress the contrast; Burhan and Itqan give the general rule for negative or confirmatory interrogatives.
  7:172/q16/p2 Naʿam could affirm the intended affirmative sense of a confirmatory question, though balā follows its negative form. — reasons: Al-Suhayli and others object to declaring naʿam disbelief; Samīn cites poetic use. Burhan distinguishes genuine inquiry from confirmation.
  7:172/q16/p3 Naʿam is ambiguous after a confirmatory negative question; balā is the safe explicit answer. — reasons: Al-Saffar, Ibn Hisham and Alusi distinguish affirmation of spoken negation from intended affirmation; Alusi prefers that Ibn Abbas meant insufficiency, not unbelief.
  7:172/q16/p4 The alif of balā is original, added after bal, or a feminine ending. — reasons: Itqan and Alusi list the three morphological accounts; the feminine analysis appeals to imāla.
7:172/q17 Who says 'we have witnessed'? [شَهِدْنَآ · referent] (turns on: Where the descendants' quoted speech ends, whether an unspoken command to angels is supplied, and how the purpose clause attaches.)
  7:172/q17/p1 The descendants themselves say it, confirming their own acknowledgment or witnessing one another. — reasons: Ibn Abbas and Ubayy are cited; Tabarsi calls this apparent because angels have not been mentioned. Ibn Ashur calls it reinforcement of balā.
  7:172/q17/p2 The angels say it after being commanded to witness. — reasons: Al-Kalbi supplies an omitted divine command; on this account a pause at balā is apt. Tabarsi objects that angels are not named.
  7:172/q17/p3 God, or God together with the angels, declares His witness. — reasons: Al-Suddi names God and angels; some give God alone. Tabari conditionally favors a raised report but doubts its wording because reliable routes stop at Ibn Amr.
  7:172/q17/p4 It begins a new divine report, 'We testify,' anticipating Judgment-day speech. — reasons: The author of the Nazm ends the covenant dialogue at balā and makes the next clause God's present witnessing; al-Jurjani invokes a poetic present use of shahida.
  7:172/q17/p5 Other witnesses include Adam or the seven heavens and earth. — reasons: Ubayy's version has God call them as witnesses; Study Quran notes variants naming Adam, heaven, earth and God.
7:172/q18 Where may one pause around 'balā' and 'we have witnessed'? [بَلَىٰ شَهِدْنَآ · grammar] (turns on: Identification of the speaker of shahidnā and the resulting syntactic attachment of an taqūlū.)
  7:172/q18/p1 Pause after balā because the descendants' speech ends there. — reasons: This follows readings that make angels or God speak shahidnā; Wāḥidī, Qurtubi and Ibn al-Jawzi explain the division. Burhan notes a general preference for stopping at balā.
  7:172/q18/p2 Do not pause after balā because shahidnā is the descendants' continued speech. — reasons: Wāḥidī says the purpose clause then attaches to 'He made them testify'; Tabari's mutual-witness reading needs the confession to continue.
7:172/q19 How does 'lest you say' attach grammatically? [أَن تَقُولُوا۟ · grammar] (turns on: The speaker of shahidnā and whether the suppressed element is a negation, fear or aversion, or an implied remembering command.)
  7:172/q19/p1 It gives the purpose of witnessing or taking the covenant: lest people later plead ignorance. — reasons: Kufans supply omitted lā, compared with 16:15 and al-Qutami's poem; Basrans supply a noun or verb expressing aversion or fear, compared with 4:176. Ibn Ashur supplies a causal lām and implied negation.
  7:172/q19/p2 It attaches specifically to 'He made them testify,' when descendants speak shahidnā. — reasons: Abu Bakr calls this clearer; Wāḥidī says attaching to the descendants' 'we testified' would make them the excuse makers, though Samīn allows one group to testify about another.
  7:172/q19/p3 It depends on an implied command to remember, mention, or explain the covenant. — reasons: Alusi finds this elegant, while calling attachment to witnessing the apparent syntax.
7:172/q20 How is 'that you say' read? [أَن تَقُولُوا۟ · readings] (turns on: Whether the clause continues third-person narrative or turns to those addressed in the covenant dialogue.)
  7:172/q20/p1 Most readers use second-person taqūlū, directly addressing the covenant people. — reasons: The direct divine question motivates the shift. Makkī prefers it for sound meaning and majority use; Ibn Ashur calls it change of addressee rather than iltifāt.
  7:172/q20/p2 Abu Amr and other reported readers use third-person yaqūlū, continuing narration about descendants. — reasons: Abu Ali cites preceding third-person wording and their response; Ibn Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and others are additionally named. Both verbs in 7:172–173 usually agree in person.
7:172/q21 What ignorance is forestalled by 'we were heedless of this'? [إِنَّا كُنَّا عَنْ هَٰذَا غَٰفِلِينَ · referent] (turns on: Whether 'this' points to a remembered primordial event or to recognized evidence of the Creator.)
  7:172/q21/p1 Ignorance of the covenant and acknowledgment of God's lordship. — reasons: The report and prophetic reminder disclose an event people may forget; Awf says they will remember it on Resurrection Day.
  7:172/q21/p2 Ignorance of God's identity as Creator and sole Lord because the proofs had not alerted people. — reasons: Baydawi and Nasafi make heedlessness lack of alerti
<<part 1 ends; continues in part 2>>

7:172/q22 How does the covenant establish proof despite forgotten testimony? [أَن تَقُولُوا۟ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ إِنَّا كُنَّا عَنْ هَٰذَا غَٰفِلِينَ · theology] (turns on: Whether an unremembered primordial pledge, present innate knowledge, or a messenger's renewed disclosure supplies binding evidence.)
  7:172/q22/p1 The original pledge binds, and prophetic reminders or innate knowledge restore its force despite forgetting the scene. — reasons: Al-Turtushi compares a forgotten witnessed divorce; Wāḥidī and Baghawī stress a truthful miracle-bearing messenger. Defenders say essential knowledge persists although the occasion fades; Tabatabai says resurrection removes worldly veils.
  7:172/q22/p2 The proof is innate reason, self-awareness and evident signs present in earthly life. — reasons: Creation shows a governor; an adult can infer God from self and world. Ibn Kathir argues this is independent of accepting an otherwise deniable report, and Tabatabai says everyone senses dependence regardless of status.
  7:172/q22/p3 A forgotten pre-birth event cannot justly ground responsibility. — reasons: Mu'tazilites and Tabarsi argue an intelligent multitude should remember such testimony, else transmigration becomes plausible; unintelligent particles cannot pledge. Tabatabai asks whether accountability rests on vanished reason, bare recognition, or forgotten words, and says ordinary worldly causes suffice.
  7:172/q22/p4 Responsibility for basic monotheism holds even without a prophet; the prophetic message adds a second proof. — reasons: Islahi says innate guidance leaves no excuse; later revelation doubles responsibility. Biqai instead says mercy delayed accountability until messengers came.
7:172/q23 What does the testimony prevent people from saying on Judgment Day? [أَن تَقُولُوا۟ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ · interpretation]
  7:172/q23/p1 They cannot plead ignorance of God's lordship or blame inherited association of partners. — reasons: The next verse gives the ancestral excuse; the witnesses and later reminders block both. Some sources specifically apply this to Arab polytheists.
7:172/q24 What does the covenant report say about predestination and deeds? [أَخَذَ رَبُّكَ ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ · theology] (turns on: Whether differentiation at the extraction defines individual fate and how divine decree relates to human choice and justice.)
  7:172/q24/p1 God divided descendants into people of Paradise and Fire, and enables each to perform the deeds of the assigned destination. — reasons: Umar and other reports answer the challenge 'what are deeds for?' with facilitation until death; versions mention right and left, white and black, two handfuls, fixed lifespans and provision. Tirmidhi grades Umar's route hasan but notes disconnection.
  7:172/q24/p2 Decreed outcomes and human choice coexist because choice is part of the complete causes of destiny. — reasons: Tabatabai cites 2:148 and 7:29–30: destinations call for fitting acts, while human choice is a partial cause. Umar responds that people should strive.
  7:172/q24/p3 The reported allotment is not injustice because God knows what each person will do and is answerable to none. — reasons: Nahhas appeals to foreknowledge; Ibn al-Arabi says creator and creatures cannot be judged by identical limits and all acts belong to God.
  7:172/q24/p4 The verse itself gives a common covenant, while destiny reports add a distinct feature. — reasons: Ibn Ashur says Malik's report explains an implication or adds material elicited by a question; Study Quran prefers universal potential for spiritual attainment.
7:172/q25 What distinct covenants or reminders accompanied the acknowledgment? [أَلَسْتُ بِرَبِّكُمْ · reports] (turns on: Whether the verse's lordship covenant alone is in view, or reports and related verses add prophetic, communal or Imamic obligations.)
  7:172/q25/p1 God promised messengers and books to remind humanity of the first pledge and warn against shirk. — reasons: Ubayy's report and variants say prophets were sent as reminders; some connect 30:30, 53:56 and 7:102 with the covenant.
  7:172/q25/p2 Prophets received an additional covenant to convey revelation and messengership. — reasons: Ubayy describes them shining like lamps and relates this separate charge to 33:7; Tustari likewise describes taking prophets from Adam's loins.
  7:172/q25/p3 The universal direct covenant grounds later particular covenants with prophets and religious communities. — reasons: Study Quran lists believers, Abraham, Israelites, Christians and People of the Book, and distinguishes later mediated obligations.
  7:172/q25/p4 Some early Twelver reports add affirmation of Muhammad and the Imams, with only some accepting the Imams. — reasons: Tabatabai also reports an Imami shadow-world test and an acknowledgment conditioned by divine love or hatred.
7:172/q26 What do the reports say about Adam, David, and the displayed descendants? [ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ · reports] (turns on: The reports differ in numerical details of lifespan and what inequalities Adam observed.)
  7:172/q26/p1 Adam gave David forty years from his thousand-year life after seeing David's light, then forgot or denied it at death. — reasons: Versions give David sixty years before the gift, record it while the pens were wet, or say Adam died at 960; descendants inherit forgetfulness and denial. Al-Tirmidhi grades the Abu Hurayra report hasan sahih.
  7:172/q26/p2 Adam gave David forty years from a lifespan reported in another form as sixty years. — reasons: One Ibn Kathir route phrases Adam's own allotted years as sixty, diverging from the widely reported thousand; variants are kept separate by their numerical detail.
  7:172/q26/p3 God varied descendants' wealth, appearance or afflictions so that people would give thanks. — reasons: Adam asked why they were unequal; God said He loved to be thanked. Some versions specify illness, poverty or outward appearance.
7:172/q27 How sound are the reports used to explain the verse? [* · reports] (turns on: Whether reports are raised or stopped, whether chains include missing or unknown transmitters, and whether broad agreement outweighs variants.)
  7:172/q27/p1 The Umar report has a broken or uncertain chain but is graded hasan or supported by other routes. — reasons: Abu Umar and Tirmidhi say Muslim ibn Yasar did not hear from Umar; Yahya ibn Ma'in questions Muslim and Nu'aym. Qurtubi accepts its meaning from other routes; Ibn Kathir explains Malik's omitted intermediary and Darqutni prefers corroborating versions.
  7:172/q27/p2 The extraction-and-address wording is more securely a Companion statement than a Prophetic report. — reasons: Tabari notes reliable transmitters stop at Abdullah ibn Amr; Ibn Kathir prefers Ibn Abbas and Ibn Amr stopped versions. Al-Hakim calls the raised Ibn Abbas chain sound, but Ibn Kathir says stronger and more numerous versions stop there.
  7:172/q27/p3 The numerous extraction reports support a real covenant in broad meaning, despite individual transmission issues. — reasons: Qurtubi cites several Companions; Tabatabai says Sunni and Shi'i routes make semantic mass transmission plausible. Ibn Kathir accepts extraction and division but separates them from the explicit testimony wording.
  7:172/q27/p4 The wording 'He showed them Himself' is preferable to 'He showed them His creation.' — reasons: Tabatabai suspects al-Ma'ani paraphrased the former to avoid corporeality; he prefers al-Kafi and al-Ayyashi, and denies corporeality follows. One narration supports literal witnessing.
7:172/q28 What happens to children who die before later responsibility? [ذُرِّيَّتَهُمْ · theology] (turns on: Whether the first acknowledgment benefited every child equally or the sincerity of the primordial response affects their outcome.)
  7:172/q28/p1 They remain on the first covenant and fitra, with Paradise or purity attributed to them. — reasons: Ibn Abbas distinguishes the first covenant from the later accountable pledge; Muqatil and Qurtubi extend this to children of polytheists. Al-Hasan's circle says their Paradise bliss rewards primordial faith.
  7:172/q28/p2 Unwilling testimony does not benefit children of the wretched. — reasons: Wāḥidī records opponents of Muqatil's view who argue the wretched confessed under compulsion.
  7:172/q28/p3 Children of polytheists serve Paradise's people because they never reached their parents' shirk. — reasons: A report from Anas gives this particular outcome while retaining their first-covenant status.
7:172/q29 How is the Black Stone connected with the covenant? [وَأَشْهَدَهُمْ · reports] (turns on: Whether its benefit is intrinsic, only obedient imitation, or covenantal testimony by God's leave.)
  7:172/q29/p1 The covenant record was placed in the Stone, which witnesses or will testify for those touching it rightly. — reasons: Ali says it can benefit and harm by God's Book; reports give it eyes and a tongue at Judgment. Fatima bint Husayn and Ja'far call touching it fulfillment of the pledge.
  7:172/q29/p2 The Stone itself cannot harm or benefit; Umar kisses it because the Prophet did. — reasons: Ali answers Umar with the covenant-witness account.

  7:172/q30/p1 It is permissible or futile as a means of preventing a decreed life: every covenanted person will emerge. — reasons: Ali ibn Husayn applied the verse to the practice; reports say a decreed child would be born even if seed fell on a stone.
